newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU oil product draw offers scant margin comfort.
newsitem.headline: EU oil product draw offers scant margin comfort.

text.p: A draw of all oil products in the European Union in June offered some comfort for margins, but a number of caveats and a large fall in crude inventories ensured the bullishness was only slight.
"It takes some pressure off, but the picture is still relatively pessimistic," said Cindy Poynter of oil consultants Bonner and Moore.

The biggest surprise for June was a fall, albeit small, of middle distillate stocks. They fell by 1.65 million barrels, or 0.5 percent, in the European Union and Norway to 314.40 million barrels, Euroilstock said in its latest monthly report.
However, this still left them 15.15 million barrels, or 5.1 percent, higher than a year ago.

Month-on-month, the fall was greatest in Germany, where stocks declined by a sizeable 6.37 million barrels. Some traders suggested in June that wholesalers and consumers engaged in restocking, partly as temperatures dropped and partly as the price fell.

"We can probably assume a large part of the draw was to consumers, but it's not likely that much of it was burnt up even in the mild weather. It's more a stock movement than a stock draw," said Geoff Pyne, oil economist at UBS.
Gasoline inventories were also off, as expected. They dropped by 2.89 million barrels, or 1.8 percent, in June to 158.10 million barrels, leaving a year-on-year shortfall of 11.05 million barrels.
For some, the fall during one of the peak months of gasoline demand was, however, smaller than normal.
"If you strip out the seasonality, it comes across as a build," said Pyne.
Crude and oil product stocks combined fell by 18.62 million barrels, or 1.7 percent, to 1,059.89 million barrels at the end of June.

Crude contributed most to the fall, dropping by 11.61 million barrels, or 2.7 percent, in June to 416.90 million barrels, leaving them 8.91 million barrels, or 2.1 percent, lower than year-ago levels.
Analysts mostly expected a fall. It was, they said likely to have been the result of Iraq's suspension of oil exports from June 8 and a high level of North Sea maintenance.
However, a number were surprised by its magnitude.
"The evidence points towards a fall, but (the size) was quite surprising," said Leslie Owens of Petroleum
Higher crude refinery intake also contributed to the draw. The utilisation rate rose to 90.57 in June from 88.48 in May.
A full inventory list, including country-by-country data, in barrels and tonnes, is on Reuters pages EUROILA to EUROILJ.
